The growth kinetics are unknown: find the rate law that explains the data.

  E1 (20 h): u1 (1/h) 0.2 from 0 h; u2 (g/L) 15.0 from 0 h. Biomass x1 5.09 -> 6.40 (max 6.57 at 15 h); substrate x2 0.01 -> 0.37 (max 0.63 at 2 h).
  E2 (20 h): u1 (1/h) 0.05 from 0 h, 0.15 from 10 h; u2 (g/L) 35.0 from 0 h, 10.0 from 10 h. Biomass x1 1.99 -> 4.15 (max 6.97 at 10 h); substrate x2 0.00 -> 0.12 (max 0.46 at 1 h).

Balance equations (given):
  dx1/dt = (r - u1 - theta4)*x1
  dx2/dt = -r*x1/theta3 + u1*(u2 - x2)

  r: specific rate in the biomass and substrate balance equations [1 / h] unknown, to be supplied by a rate law
  u1: dilution factor [1 / h] 
  u2: substrate concentration in the feed [g / l] 
  x1: measured concentration [g / l] 
  x2: substrate concentration [g / l] 
  t: time [h]

answer.reasoning: None of the fitted candidates fits within the noise: each exceeds its 95% chi-square limit, and the Andrews and exponential-inhibition fits also show poorly separable parameters. The recurring E3 substrate under-prediction at high glucose suggests testing stronger high-substrate inhibition. I also include a biomass-stimulatory law as a distinct mechanism to check whether biomass dependence helps explain the differing experiments.

candidates.reason: Test the higher-order substrate-inhibition form: stronger suppression at high substrate may address the E3 substrate under-prediction. Its extra parameters may be difficult to identify, so check their intervals and correlations.
Test Monod growth with a finite-substrate cutoff. This provides a different inhibition shape from the Andrews and exponential forms already tried.

Test biomass-stimulatory kinetics as a distinct biomass-dependence mechanism. Compare its fit across experiments, especially whether it improves biomass predictions without worsening the E3 substrate misfit.
